title: Rabboni (John 20:11–18)
hookLine: Mary turns at her name, and becomes the apostle to the apostles

lines: TWO ANGELS, AND GRIEF LOUDER THAN WONDER.
cards: The two men have gone home. Mary Magdalene hasn't. She stands outside the tomb, crying.
She stoops and looks in, and there are two angels in white, sitting where the body had been, one at the head and one at the feet. They ask: woman, why are you weeping?
She answers as if angels were the most ordinary thing in the world, because grief is louder than wonder. They have taken away my Lord, and I don't know where they've laid him.
Then she turns around, and someone is standing there.

teach.b: She doesn't recognize him. John says she supposed him to be the gardener. Sir, she says, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him away.
Then one word. In the King James Bible: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master."
Rabboni: my teacher. Her name. That's all it takes.

Back in chapter ten, he said the good shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice. Here it happens. Then something people have puzzled over: "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father."
In Latin, noli me tangere, and painters loved it. The Greek may mean something closer to stop clinging to me: there's somewhere to go and a message to carry. Go to my brothers.
So she goes, and in the Greek she says it in her own voice: I have seen the Lord. She's the first person in John's Gospel to see the risen Jesus, and the first sent to tell.
Christian tradition calls her the apostle to the apostles. In 2016, Pope Francis raised her day, July twenty-second, to a full feast.
Orthodox Christians call her equal to the apostles. One more thing worth clearing up: the idea that Mary Magdalene was a reformed prostitute isn't in the Gospels.
It grew from a sixth-century sermon that merged her with other women. The Gospels remember her as a witness.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles; many churches read this passage during the Easter season.

o: my teacher, the name Mary knew him by
my friend, a greeting among equals
my Lord and God, a cry of worship

games.q: what's inside John 20:11–18 — tap the pairs.

s: the Gospels say Mary Magdalene was a prostitute
they don't. the idea grew from a sixth-century sermon that merged her with other women.
in John, Mary Magdalene is the first to see the risen Jesus
and the first sent to tell the others.
Mary recognizes Jesus when she first sees him
she supposes he's the gardener, until he says her name.

games.q: you're Mary, weeping at the tomb. a man you take for the gardener asks why you're crying. what do you say?
o: sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him.
games.why: she asks the gardener for the body, and then he says one word: Mary. she turns: Rabboni.

practice: Remember being called by name by someone who loved you, a parent at the door, a friend across a crowded room, and hear your name in their voice.
If you're a Christian, you can say Mary's words quietly, I have seen the Lord; if not, name something good you've seen with your own eyes this week, and say, I have seen that.

wordCard.voice: Rabboni. My teacher, my master: what Mary says when she hears her name and turns.

orig.note: Greek spelling of a Semitic word that John translates as master, teacher.

carryVoice: Your line: I have seen the lord. It started with one word: her own name. Another week, done.
